lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you met first and third person. Which words does a first-person narrator use? I, me and we.
The narrator is the voice telling the story. Their point of view shapes what we learn and how we feel.
A first-person narrator is in the story (I, we). We only know what they see, think and feel, and they might not be fair to others.
A third-person narrator is outside the story (he, she, they). Some tell us what everyone thinks; others follow just one character.
The same event told by two narrators can feel very different. A spilt drink might be a disaster to one character and a joke to another.
Try it in the world: tell your last game adventure twice: once as yourself (I), and once as your buddy or pet would tell it. What changes? Next: figurative language.

exercises.prompt: What is a narrator?
exercises.explain: The narrator is the voice that tells the story.

exercises.prompt: Which words show a first-person narrator?
exercises.hint: The narrator is in the story.
exercises.explain: A first-person narrator says I and we.

exercises.prompt: A first-person narrator is a character in the story.
exercises.explain: Yes: they take part in the story.

exercises.prompt: "She crept into the kitchen." Which point of view is this?
exercises.explain: "She" shows a narrator outside the story: third person.

exercises.prompt: "I crept into the kitchen." Which point of view is this?
exercises.explain: "I" shows a first-person narrator.

exercises.prompt: What can a first-person narrator NOT know for sure?
exercises.explain: They only know their own thoughts.

exercises.prompt: "My little brother ruined everything, as usual." What does this show about the narrator?
exercises.hint: Look at the words "ruined" and "as usual". Are they fair?
choices: They may not be fair to the brother.
exercises.explain: The narrator's feelings colour how they tell it.

exercises.prompt: A narrator tells us what Kai, Zara and their teacher are all thinking. What kind of narrator is it?
exercises.hint: Outside the story, seeing into every mind.
exercises.explain: A third-person narrator who knows everyone's thoughts.

exercises.prompt: The same event can feel different when told by a different narrator.
exercises.explain: Yes: each narrator sees it their own way.

exercises.prompt: Why might an author choose a first-person narrator?
choices: to let us share one character's feelings closely
exercises.explain: We see everything through one character's eyes and feelings.

exercises.prompt: Zara drops the cake. Told by Zara: "The worst day ever." Told by her dog: "Best. Day. Ever." What does this show?
choices: The narrator changes how an event feels.
exercises.explain: The same event feels different to each narrator.

exercises.prompt: A third-person narrator follows only Kai. What will we mostly learn?
choices: what Kai sees, thinks and feels
exercises.explain: We see the story through Kai's experience.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence shows the narrator's opinion?
choices: The mean old guard wouldn't let us in.
The guard stood at the gate.
exercises.explain: "Mean" is the narrator's opinion of the guard.

exercises.prompt: A narrator always tells us everything fairly.
exercises.explain: No: a narrator can be unfair or not know everything.

exercises.prompt: How would "The Three Little Pigs" change if the wolf told it?
choices: We might hear why the wolf acted as he did.
It would be exactly the same.
exercises.explain: We would hear the wolf's side of the story.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: first person or third person?
exercises.hint: Look for I, we and my, or she, they and his.
exercises.explain: I, we and my show a narrator inside the story: first person. She, they and his show a narrator outside it: third person.

exercises.prompt: Match each narrator to what they can tell us.
matches: only their own thoughts, as I
exercises.hint: Can the narrator see into other minds?
exercises.explain: A first-person narrator knows only their own thoughts. An all-knowing third-person narrator tells everyone's. A third-person narrator who follows one character tells what that character sees and feels.

exercises.prompt: Tell "She crept into the kitchen" in the first person: put the words in order.
exercises.hint: A first-person narrator tells the story as I.
exercises.explain: I crept into the kitchen. She becomes I, because now the narrator is the one in the story.

exercises.prompt: Zara tells the story as I. Sort what she can know.
exercises.hint: Zara is inside the story: she only knows her own mind.
exercises.explain: Zara knows what she sees, hears and feels. She can only guess what her dog thinks or what Kai secretly plans: she is not inside their heads.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: a fact, or the narrator's opinion?
items: The guard stood at the gate.
It was the worst day ever.
exercises.hint: Look for words that judge, like mean, silly or worst.
exercises.explain: Facts say what happened: the guard stood there, the paint was spilt, the gate was shut. Opinions show the narrator's feelings: mean, silly, the worst day ever.

exercises.prompt: Zara drops a cake. Match each narrator to how they would tell it.
exercises.hint: Think about what the cake meant to each one.
exercises.explain: Zara, who dropped it, feels it is the worst day ever. The dog, who ate it, thinks it is the best day ever. Mum, who baked it, sees her hard work gone: one event, three points of view.

exercises.prompt: How many first-person words are in "We ran, but I fell, and my knee hurt, so Kai helped me"?
exercises.hint: Find every I, me, my, we, us and our.
exercises.explain: We, I, my and me are first-person words: 4. Kai is a name: someone else in the story with the narrator.
